title: CuTe Tensors: Structure and Operations in GPU Kernels
key_concepts: Memory spaces: GMEM, SMEM, RMEM, TMEM
Data movement: copying between memory spaces
critical_patterns: Load → Compute → Store: Efficient data handling through memory hierarchy
Double Buffering: Overlapping computation with data transfer
constraints: Cannot allocate new tensors inside @cute.kernel functions
Alignment is crucial for performance and correctness
Dynamic layouts may incur runtime overhead
Avoid accessing tensors across thread blocks
compressed_summary: CuTe DSL provides a structured approach to handling tensors on GPUs, where a tensor is defined by a pointer, layout, and metadata. Tensors in CuTe enable automatic bounds checking, compile-time address optimization, and type-safe operations. They can reside in various memory spaces: GMEM for large data, SMEM for fast block-shared access, RMEM for thread-private fast access, and TMEM for Blackwell-specific operations. Creating tensors involves specifying a data pointer and layout, and they can be converted from framework tensors using DLPack for zero-copy integration. Tensors support operations like indexing, slicing, reshaping, and partitioning, which are crucial for efficient GPU computations. Partitioning allows dividing tensors among threads or blocks, facilitating operations like GEMM. Data movement between memory spaces is managed through copy operations, with synchronization needed after shared memory writes. Common patterns include Load → Compute → Store, Double Buffering for pipelining, and Reduction for accumulation. Best practices emphasize using DLPack for integration, aligning tensors for performance, and minimizing global memory access. Avoid allocating tensors in kernels, ignoring alignment, or accessing tensors across thread blocks. Debugging involves printing tensor information and visualizing layouts. Advanced users can define custom tensor types for specialized use cases. Overall, CuTe tensors are composable, transformable, and optimized for GPU kernel development, with a focus on memory hierarchy and efficient data handling.
